headline: Free MIT Sky Renderer for Three.js Catches a Paid Product Mid-Build
lede: Su (jeantimex), a Google software engineer, has ported the @takram/three-geospatial library's React Three Fiber demos to Vanilla JavaScript, making photorealistic atmospheric scattering and volumetric clouds available to any Three.js project without framework dependencies. The underlying library was built by Tokyo design firm Takram under a Japanese government contract and is now the most technically complete free sky-rendering engine in the Three.js ecosystem. Its prominence carries an awkward subplot: a Three.js educator had been building a paid product to fill exactly this gap — and discovered, mid-development, that it was already filled.
body:
Su (jeantimex), an engineer at Google (GOOGL), released the Vanilla JS port alongside a live interactive globe demo hosted on GitHub Pages. The original **@takram/three-geospatial** package ships its showcase scenes in *React Three Fiber* (R3F), a React-based wrapper that abstracts Three.js's scene graph into JSX components. By rewriting the demos as plain TypeScript with Vite, Su removed that dependency entirely, extending the effects to the far larger population of Three.js developers who work without React. The port covers two flagship packages: **@takram/three-atmosphere**, which renders physically accurate skies, aerial perspective, and sun-and-moon lighting, and **@takram/three-clouds**, which adds geospatial volumetric cloud layers.

The library was created by Shota Matsuda, a director and design engineer at Takram — a Tokyo design consultancy — and its origin was practical rather than hobbyist. Takram was commissioned by Eukarya, a Japanese Web GIS startup, to build the rendering engine for PLATEAU VIEW 3.0, a digital-twin city platform developed under Japan's Cabinet Office *SBIR* (Small Business Innovation Research) program. Takram's formal contribution concluded in March 2025, and the codebase was published as MIT-licensed open source. Garrett Johnson, a former NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory systems engineer who worked on Mars Helicopter and Perseverance rover tooling and now consults independently on 3D graphics, is the second listed contributor; his involvement is structural — three-geospatial is explicitly designed to interoperate with his **3DTilesRendererJS** library, which streams Google's Photorealistic 3D Tiles into Three.js scenes.

The library implements *precomputed atmospheric scattering*, a technique codified by French researcher Eric Bruneton in a 2008 paper and widely adopted in real-time rendering engines. The method precomputes the physics of light traveling through a planetary atmosphere — *Rayleigh scattering* (which gives clear skies their blue color and sunsets their red), *Mie scattering* (which produces haze and the sun's soft corona), and ozone absorption — into a compact set of lookup textures that can be queried at runtime with fewer than ten texture fetches per pixel. The clouds layer adds a separate *raymarching* pass, tracing rays through a density volume to simulate light traveling through cloud matter, with **Beer Shadow Maps** handling sun-perspective shadowing and a 16× *temporal upscaling* step that reconstructs full-resolution frames from a fraction of the raymarching work, keeping the effect interactive in a browser.

The thread opens with Dan Greenheck, a Three.js educator who runs threejsroadmap.com, noting that he had been building Three.js Sky Pro — described on the product page as “a production-ready sky rendering engine” with volumetric clouds, atmospheric scattering, and a tuning GUI, sold as a turnkey package. Mid-development, he searched for existing solutions and found @takram/three-geospatial. His post reads as genuinely conflicted: he had been aware of the library but had underestimated its feature completeness. The episode illustrates a recurring dynamic in open-source graphics tooling: a commercial niche can close quietly when a well-resourced government project publishes its rendering engine as a free library.

Photorealistic atmosphere rendering has been technically feasible in browsers for several years but remained locked behind game-engine pipelines or expensive hand-rolled *WebGL* code. Three-geospatial brings the full stack — physically based sky, volumetric clouds with light shafts, aerial perspective — into the modular npm ecosystem alongside the broader Three.js and *3D Tiles* toolchain. With an active *WebGPU* rewrite under way in the takram repository, the next iteration should be able to offload cloud raymarching to compute shaders, closing the remaining performance gap with native applications. Su's Vanilla JS port removes the last practical friction: you no longer need React to put a photorealistic sky in a browser.

concepts.definition: A popular React-based wrapper around Three.js that allows developers to describe a 3D scene graph using JSX components instead of imperative JavaScript. It simplifies scene management and state handling but adds React as a hard dependency, excluding developers who work with plain JavaScript or TypeScript outside a React project.

A real-time rendering technique that pre-bakes the physics of sunlight traveling through a planetary atmosphere into a small set of lookup textures. At runtime, sky color, aerial perspective, and ground illumination are retrieved via cheap texture samples rather than expensive per-frame simulation, making physically accurate skies practical in games and browsers.

The elastic scattering of light by atmospheric particles far smaller than the light's wavelength — chiefly nitrogen and oxygen molecules. Because shorter (blue) wavelengths scatter more strongly, the sky appears blue during the day and the sun appears red or orange near the horizon, where light must travel through more atmosphere.

The scattering of light by particles comparable in size to the light's wavelength — aerosols, dust, and water droplets. Unlike Rayleigh scattering it is roughly wavelength-independent, producing the white glow of haze, the soft corona around the sun, and the milky appearance of humid or polluted air.

A rendering technique that steps a ray through a 3D volume — such as a cloud density field — sampling the medium at intervals to accumulate color and opacity. It produces realistic volumetric effects that traditional polygon rasterization cannot represent, at the cost of many GPU samples per pixel.

A volumetric shadowing technique that extends standard shadow mapping by storing the optical depth (Beer-Lambert transmittance) of a volume as seen from the light source. Used in cloud rendering to determine how much sunlight is attenuated as it passes through cloud layers, producing realistic self-shadowing and the darkening of clouds from within.

A GPU technique that reconstructs a high-resolution frame by accumulating information from multiple lower-resolution frames over time, using motion vectors to align them. It allows an expensive render effect — such as cloud raymarching — to run at a fraction of full resolution each frame while still producing a high-quality result.

The browser graphics API, based on OpenGL ES, that enables GPU-accelerated 2D and 3D rendering in web pages without plugins. Three.js has traditionally targeted WebGL; it is now being supplemented by WebGPU, which exposes more modern GPU features including compute shaders.

The modern browser graphics and compute API that succeeds WebGL, exposing lower-level GPU features including compute shaders — which allow general-purpose GPU workloads beyond rendering. WebGPU enables techniques like cloud raymarching to run as standalone compute passes, with significant performance potential over the equivalent WebGL approach.

A government program, used in both the US and Japan, that awards contracts and grants to small businesses for R&D with potential public benefit. In Japan's Cabinet Office program, Eukarya received SBIR funding to build PLATEAU VIEW, a digital-twin city platform — the project that commissioned Takram to develop three-geospatial.

An open standard for streaming massive 3D geospatial datasets — city models, terrain, point clouds — to a renderer on demand, in a hierarchical level-of-detail structure. Google's Photorealistic 3D Tiles uses this format to deliver its global city and terrain data; the 3DTilesRendererJS library brings this streaming capability to Three.js scenes.

repos.summary: A MIT-licensed TypeScript and GLSL monorepo by Takram Design Engineering that adds production-quality geospatial rendering to Three.js and React Three Fiber. Its flagship packages implement precomputed atmospheric scattering (@takram/three-atmosphere) and volumetric cloud rendering with Beer Shadow Maps and temporal upscaling (@takram/three-clouds). Originally commissioned for Japan's Cabinet Office digital-twin platform, it is now the most complete free sky-rendering library in the Three.js ecosystem.

A Vanilla JavaScript and TypeScript port of the @takram/three-geospatial demo scenes by Google engineer Su (jeantimex) that removes the React Three Fiber dependency entirely. It ships an interactive 3D globe with atmospheric scattering and volumetric cloud effects runnable as plain HTML with Vite, with no React required. The accompanying live demo at jeantimex.github.io/geospatial shows the full atmosphere-and-clouds stack in a browser.

A Three.js-compatible renderer for the Cesium 3D Tiles format, developed under NASA's AMMOS program by Garrett Johnson, that streams large-scale geospatial datasets — terrain, city photogrammetry, point clouds — into a browser-based 3D scene. Three-geospatial is explicitly designed to interoperate with it, making the two libraries a complementary stack for browser-based digital twins. It supports Three.js, Babylon.js, and R3F targets.
